utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. We'll continue with the evidence of Mr. Mladenovski, who will now be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined, that is, examined by other counsel. Please remember that the solemn declaration to speak the truth, which you gave yesterday at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovski.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman, I represent General Pavkovic. I'm going to ask you just a few questions this afternoon. I think if you listen very carefully to the question, make sure you understand it before you try to answer it, we'll get through this rather quickly, okay. Okay. I saw you nod --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us -- could you tell us where you work now, what you're doing now in your life.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 31st of December, 2006, I stopped working in the army, my service was terminated, that is to say I retired as of the 1st of January, 2007. I'm currently employed. I work on the project of digitalization of the military archives. This project is conducted by non-governmental organization called Jefferson Institute, and I have contract-type work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I assume that involves scanning documents and turning them into computerized documents basically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can go on to something else. Do you know a Professor Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So neither he nor anyone else on his behalf has contacted you and asked you for any samples of your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've not provided any samples of your handwriting to anyone for the use of Professor Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we were to ask you to provide handwriting samples for use of an expert witness that we might want to call, would you be willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here in this court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably wouldn't, not only to you but to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd like 3D1130 then brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, do you wish to tell us why you would not wish to give handwriting samples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question that was put to me whether I would be willing, whether I would wish to provide samples, if I were to be explained why I should give handwriting samples my answer was that I probably wouldn't. However, if it concerns something that I had done, if it were explained to me, if it was necessary to compare to something that I had done previously, then I would provide samples. This is why my answer was: I probably wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if we wanted to have our handwriting expert compare your handwriting samples to the writing that you say on this exhibit, 1130, that we should be looking at right now, we wanted him to be able to make those comparisons with handwriting samples from you. Would you then be willing to give him handwriting samples at his direction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, yes. If that involved a specific case, just as I have described to His Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The specific case is the document we're looking at on the screen, so I take it you'd no objection if Mr. Visnjic gave me your contact details so that we can accomplish that, true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on, Mr. Ackerman, if you have some further procedure in mind, as I know you may from notification given to us, then is there a particular reason why samples cannot be taken here? Have they to be taken in particular circumstances or can you not make use of the presence of the witness to deal with the matter and speed things up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not an expert and I wouldn't know what kind of samples my expert would want to take, what kinds of things he'd want him to write. I assume it would be a series of numbers, but I would really not want to substitute myself for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As long as you bear in mind the urgency of the situation, then we are content.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it can be done pretty quickly, Your Honour, once he returns to Belgrade and we do have our witness organized and prepared I think to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Poised and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so. I shouldn't make broad statements like that, but I think that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to leave for two minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to leave for two minutes out of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're now looking at 3D1130. Now, I take it this document comes from the archives, that's where it came from; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how is it you can tell that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these are archive lists which are kept in the military museum together with other documents. Secondly, I see that on page 1 in the upper right corner there is the inventory number that is assigned at the military archives. Then at the end on page 8, yet again I see and recognise my signature, which means that I reviewed this on behalf of the military archives and I received this list together with other documents myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The reason I asked the question is because you indicate in your statement that -- that there are three or four copies made of the document once you have completed your work with it and it has been given a number, and what -- what I'd like to know from you is: Are all of those copies, three or four, all kept in the archive or do copies go out of the archive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Archive lists are produced in three copies in principle. One copy, the original, accompanies original documents and it all constitutes a pile, a set of documents, a bundle; and then one copy remains in the military archives and is used as a source of information in order not to go back to the original bundle every time; and the last copy is returned to the unit which had originally submitted the documents. If this involves a small unit, if this is some independent unit, then a fourth copy is produced for that lower-level unit. But as a said, as a rule it is made in three copies, one, the original, remains in the bundle in the original set; the second copy remains within the archives and is used for information for future; and the third one is returned to the unit. All three copies need to be identical, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How do you distinguish the one that's on the screen from one that may have been returned to the unit that supplied it in the first place? How can you tell this one is from the archive rather than, say, from the General Staff? Just by looking at it can you tell?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at this photocopy I cannot say whether this is an original or not, but I think that this should be from the archives. However, based on the photocopy one can't tell -- or at least looking at the screen I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We'll talk about that a little more in just a moment. Where is the archive located physically in Serbia? Where would one find it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is located in the barracks of the military technical institute, Ratka Resanovica number 1, that's the name of the street. I think it's number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that where it was in 1999 when you were doing your work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was it then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time when we were involved in this the archive was relocated to several locations because the building where it was housed before had been damaged, so before the bombing began the archive was moved to several locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where was it you were doing your work with regard to this particular document as an example?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were housed in the military museum in Kalemegdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far is that from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kalemegdan is the prettiest part of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume I've been there then. What ministry is in control of the archive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know that. I know that for some time the archives was directly within the ministry, and then at some point it was part of the General Staff but I wouldn't be able to tell you at which time it belonged to which institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you don't know that in 1999, for instance, and 2000, 2001, through that period that it was under control of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about security arrangements at the archive, can anyone just walk in and start looking through documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, people can't just walk in. There are people who are authorised to handle archive material, they are tasked with it and they work on it, and then everybody else who would like to gain access to enter have to have a special authorisation, which means that they cannot go into the depot where the archive material is; but rather, they need to approach administrators first and gain access. In the archive building there is a reading room and archive material can be made available there upon prior authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is that room supervised in some way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So would it be easy for someone to come in and request certain group of archive documents and make changes in them, in the reading room; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you were doing this work that is represented by this exhibit you see in front of you, how many people were working there with you doing the same kind of work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number, but roughly there were about a dozen of us. We worked in two rooms. We separated along the smoking/non-smoking lines and we worked there under the supervision of superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you were asked by Mr. Visnjic about the two different dates that you can see there on the front of the document and you gave an explanation about that, and that raised some questions I want to ask you. First thing, you said that there was an order from the General Staff that all documents created during the war during the NATO bombing had to be prepared and handed over to the military archives for safekeeping and classification. Do you know when that order was entered, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I said yesterday that it was the General Staff. Now, I don't know whether it was, indeed, the General Staff or the ministry. The answer to your question is that I don't know because it was our superior officers who received that and we dealt with completely different matters. I don't know about that particular order, about gathering and turning over that archive material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you can just say you don't know and we can move along. You also said during that answer: "There was an enormous quantity of these documents." Do you have any idea of how many documents or pages of documents there were that were turned over created during the NATO bombing? Do you have any idea of the number?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it have been in the hundreds of thousands or in the millions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably were hundreds of thousands, but I really don't know the number because these records were kept by another person. It wasn't within our scope of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You also said in answer to that question these words: "They needed to first of all put them in the right order, then to fill in the archive lists, to pack them in bundles, after that load them on trucks. Usually the material would arrive on trucks for the most part." First of all, who is they who put them in the right order and filled them in the archive lists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was selected to prepare documents and type up lists. I don't know that. I don't know who gathered and put it in the right order and brought them, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you said they needed to put them in the right order and fill in the archive list, you must have somebody in mind. What group of people were involved in doing that, do you have any idea at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who did it in each unit, how, in which way, because I never went to assist them nor was I made aware of it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your department didn't do any of this kind of work, did it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our service had contract workers, and they were the ones providing assistance. So whenever somebody needed assistance they would get somebody from outside and they were called contract workers who were brought in to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we're having a communication problem. Somehow these documents got put together and loaded on trucks and sent to where you were working, as I understand it. Somebody organized them and put them in packages and put them on these trucks and sent them to you, and I think you've told me you don't know who did that. But I think you will tell me that this list that we have here on the screen in front of us was not made by you but made by the people who were preparing those documents to send them to you. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean, archive list that was typed up on a typewriter or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the document on your screen. That's the document I'm talking about. That wasn't prepared where you were working; it was prepared at another location, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this one came from the General Staff if you believe the stamp on the upper left-hand corner; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it came to you with all those blanks down there filled in accompanied by a stack of documents in a folder; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now if we can go rather quickly to the last page of this document. If we look down there at the bottom, doesn't it indicate who it was who actually prepared this list, warrant officer second class Miodrag Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is stated and warrant officer Miodrag Jankovic's signature is there, but I don't know whether he was the one who brought it, prepared it, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when you were contacted to provide information about this document by, I think, an investigator for Mr. Visnjic perhaps, and you gave a statement, as a matter of fact, about this document. I'm wondering if during that process where you were concerned about this document and being asked about it you had occasion to get in touch with Miodrag Jankovic and ask him if he remembered anything about it; did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it what would happen then, that you would be handed or you would get somehow this folder to have this list and a bunch of documents and your job was to go through it and check it to make sure it was all together and accurate and everything on it was correct; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we go back to the first page now, which I think we can do fairly quickly, now if we just look right there at that first entry, line number 1, you apparently made a correction there, crossed out a 2 and put in a 3; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you did that because the document represented by line 1 was not a two-page document as Mr. Jankovic had indicated but a three-page document. You counted it and said, no, no, no, this has three pages instead of two, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three leaves because this is not about pages but rather leaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What's the difference between a leaf and a page? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in archive work we deal with leaves, that's the term --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a leaf is a piece of paper that can be printed on both sides, so it can be two pages printed on both sides, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A leaf has two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then down in line 4 you crossed out a 3 and put in a 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And down in line 6 that requires you to explain that to me. Line 6 under log number and date, you seem to have crossed out a 6 and put a 5, and then you've written some other number underneath. Why'd you do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When conducting the check, and let me mention that our superior officers explained to us the procedure we were to follow, they were with us all the time. When we found any irregularities such as this one, the person who prepared this said it was 140/1 to 6 in the log-book. If I had the document before we I could show you, but in any case I established that in the log there was 140-1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 respectively, but there was an additional document numbered 217-1. So that whoever prepared this list entered the correct number of documents, but the log-book numbers did not correspond to the actual situation. I don't know whether I've explained it clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are -- I counted it and I'm not going to go through every page, but I counted 68 places just in this one document where you had to make corrections. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, if you counted 68, I can tell you there was some lists without any mistakes and there were others with 60 or 100 mistakes. It all depended on who prepared the document and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that with the war going on and the order to get all these things archived that everybody was working under a bit of pressure to try to get this work done and short-handed and working pretty hard; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the war was over by the time these lists were prepared. I think the war was already finished. As to whether they were under a bit of pressure or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you feel like you were under a bit of pressure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was in 1999, the documents started arriving. In the meantime the building where the military archive was to be housed came under renovation. We were not under any pressure. Nobody drove us to work quickly. All we had to concentrate on was to work correctly and with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If my count is correct, how could it be that Miodrag Jankovic would make 68 mistakes just in this one document if he wasn't under pressure and hurrying? What would account for that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask Jankovic that; he would probably be able to tell you. But I really don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, how many of these would you do in a day? How many folders of documents could you do in a day, do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would all depend on the number of documents in the folder. There was some with 10 documents, others with 15, others with 50, 500, or 1.000. It did not depend on me but on the number of documents in a bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That makes complete sense. Look at the one we're dealing with here I guess is a relatively small one. How long would you say it would take you to do what you did with this document, how much time would that have taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly. I'd have to see the documents, and I really don't know how much time I would have needed for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really am not looking for a precise number, but would it take you all day to do this one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you might do ten like this in a day if they were all the same size?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On condition they were put in good order and that there weren't too many corrections. Ten, yes, but if not too many corrections were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in -- over this period of time that you did this would you say you did hundreds of these folders or thousands of these folders? What would be your best guess as to how many you did?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, believe me. I haven't a clue. We worked from 1999 until we had to move back to the building where the military archives were to be housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So hundreds at least?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe more, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. At the top you told us yesterday you entered numbers there that resulted from your counting of the number of documents and the number of pages or leaves; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in this particular one you found that there were 277 documents and 735 pages; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leaves, not pages, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, leaves, yes. And how did you add these up? Did you have a machine that you added on or did you write the numbers down on paper and add them up, or how did you do the addition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I combined methods. First I went down column 5, each page from 1 to 8 - I explained this yesterday - so every page at the bottom of the page I would enter a number, up to page 8. Then I would add all these subtotals, and then we would check it with a calculator. So first we added up manually. I personally would take the first page, I would go from 1 to 6, and then I would go back from 6 to 1 in order to check my own addition. I would go down the page and then up the page, and I would do the same for column 6, the number of leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that Miodrag Jankovic apparently made 68 mistakes in one document, I guess you would concede that it was possible for you to make one or two occasionally; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, if I made a mistake the people who then took the documents over and continued working on them would notice. When the bundles were finished they were dealt with further and there would be a person who would check everything probably. I'm not absolutely sure that's what happened, but I was never told I had made any mistakes, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess what you just said is you're not sure that there was somebody who actually went into a detailed review of your work to see if you had counted correctly and things like that. I think you mentioned yesterday there was one person who got the documents after you finished who entered the archive number and did the additional work. I assume she did that for everybody who was working in your group; true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday this person was an archivist who was in charge of the complete records. After the procedure was completed there was still things to be done. I don't know precisely what or how, but to the best of my recollection she was supposed to separate out the three copies of the list, put one in the bundle, put one in the archives for information, send one back to the unit, and pack up the bundle, put it in a crate. I'm not sure what she did exactly, how she did it. I'm just assuming this is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at page 7 now, it has line 82 on it. We're going to kind of focus in on line 82 there. Now, one thing I guess must be absolutely true, and that is this was long ago and you did many of these and you do not have any specific memory of the work you did on this document at all; all you can do is look at it and draw conclusions from what you see. But in terms of your memory of actually doing this document, you have none, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all to the best of my recollection what I can see here is that I signed this list, which means that I was the one who dealt with it; secondly, there are lots of lists that were done, yes. So it's only by looking at my signature I can be sure that I did this one, and then looking at the handwriting, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at line 82, you told us yesterday that it was done wrong, that those numbers should have been written above the crossed-out numbers instead of below; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said there was an error, it was done wrong; I just said that we were told what procedure we should follow when entering these corrections. We were told that only if there was not enough room in the little box or if the number was very high up in the box and there was no room to enter a number above the number we had crossed out, only then should we write the number below the number we were correcting. And in this case I can see there was enough room to enter the number above.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, okay, then you're saying whoever did this was not following the correct procedure when they put the number below instead of above; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the receipt of this bundle, if somebody was entering corrections these had to be entered but they would have to be initialled. Whoever entered the correction would have to initial it. That's one thing. And secondly, looking at it as a lay person I think that this was done by someone who was not an expert because they forgot that the front page should also then be corrected, the one containing the total number of documents and leaves. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let me suggest something to you and just tell us whether you think this is possible or not. Before this ever got to you, it was put together by this guy, Miodrag Jankovic, who made several mistakes. Do you think it's possible that he spent a long time typing up this document, a lot of typing on here, a lot of detailed typing and stuff goes into this, spent a long time putting it together, thought he was finished with it, all of a sudden discovered he had left a document out, and rather than retype the whole thing, he just wrote in 248-2 and the number 2 and the number 5. That could have been happened, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so because then the total number of documents and leaves on the front page would have been different; that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's if somebody counted it properly. You can make a mistake counting too, can't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can make a mistake, but I don't think I did in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask just one supplementary question on that. If this proposal were correct -- or at least if this had happened and this alteration was made and the front page had been altered, if both of these things had happened, would you have accepted the document in this form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean if the numbers tallied on the front page also, the number of documents and leaves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But again, looking at all of this it doesn't look like the figures written in my handwriting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's -- I -- that's a separate question. And -- so even without an initial a person presenting the document to you can make alterations on it that you would accept as long as the figures were correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand your question correctly, that person, if they wanted to add something in my presence, I would enter the correction and initial it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but could they alter it before they brought it to you in a way that you would accept without any initial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If this had come to you with the 248-2 written in there and the number 2 and the number 5 in place of 1 and 3, you would have noticed that the numbers written on page 1 in terms of pages and documents was wrong, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not even sure I want to take the time to explain it. When you add one document and two pages, like is added at line 82, then the totals on the front page are incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But those totals on the front page are not entered by the person Miodrag Jankovic who prepares the document; those totals on the front page are only entered by you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miodrag Jankovic was supposed to enter the total number of documents and leaves when he prepared this list. As he had not entered this, our superiors explained to us that in that case we should enter this rather than sending it back for Miodrag Jankovic to do it. So they said that where a column was blank, we should enter whatever had to be entered in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to page 1 because I think we're confused but I want to make sure. All right. Up there in the upper right-hand corner there is a box, and in that box there's a date and the number of documents and the number of pages. Now, Miodrag Jankovic is supposed to put the number of documents and leaves in that before he gets it to you or is that supposed to be left blank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to enter the number of documents and leaves in these little boxes where it says documents and leaves, he and everybody else who prepared this list was supposed to do it. There were other documents where the number of documents and leaves had been entered but they were incorrect and we had to correct them. So we would correct that as well as the other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's another mistake that he made; true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, these three copies that are made of this document, did you make any effort to find any of the copies that were made of this document at the time when you were asked questions about this document by the investigator for Mr. Visnjic? Did you see if you could find any copies that had been made?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the last question I want to ask you about this document -- well, yes, the last one maybe. Should there not be a stamp on here somewhere showing receipt and the date of receipt of this document by the archive by your organization? Shouldn't that appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just some kind of a stamp that says this document was received by the archive department on such and such a date. Shouldn't there be some kind of an indication when you received it from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite honestly, I don't know because that did not fall within my sphere of work, whether the office of the military archives was supposed to enter that or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to explore a couple of mysteries now, maybe you can help me solve them. First of all, in the upper right-hand corner of this document you see there on the screen, I take it you don't see any kind of an archive stamp there, do you, a round archive stamp?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the photocopy you can't see it, and on the screen I can't see it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to now look at another document, it's 3D1108. It will show up here on your document in just a moment. And this is the copy as explained yesterday was supplied by the archive but not in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't got it yet, Mr. Ackerman. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see that? Now, that's the same document we've been looking at but it has an archive stamp, a round archive stamp. How do you explain that that one has an archive stamp and the other one didn't?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- no. I really can't explain that because the person who handed this over is the only one who can explain it. A photocopy has to be certified. Why one has the stamp and the other one doesn't, I really couldn't explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look really quickly now at 3D1131. Now, my first question is: Have you ever seen this document before to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to page 2. Now, we need to go down about halfway, it's entry number 250 and we need to blow it up as much as possible. On the right-hand side of 250 where it says -- I may have to give you a hard copy for you to be able to see -- you can probably see it now. 250 it has a stamp over there, and it indicates that it was entered in the archives of the VJ in the year 06, 2006. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's not very legible, but yes I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says 06 Godina, right? Like 06 Godina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it very well, but it does look like a 6, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it help if I showed you a hard copy just so you can be sure? Would that make it easier for you to be sure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now, it is 2006, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need to have it back now. Now, if we look over in the left-hand column we're looking at documents that have entry dates of 15 and 26 May of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So can you explain how some 2006 entry was made on this document from those earlier dates, how that happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me tell you that I don't know how this happened. As for what it says in columns 9 and 10, that means that they turned over the log-book to the military archives in 2006. Now, as to why they didn't do that earlier, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And finally I'd like you to look at IC195, that's the document you wrote on yesterday. And you see your writing there in red, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a simple question for you: Were you trying to make the 5 you made yesterday look like the one underneath it? Was that something you tried to do or did it just happen naturally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all I didn't quite understand the question put by Mr. Visnjic so I started writing 3 and that wasn't deliberate. Now, as for me correcting anything, no, I had no intention of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question from the Bench. Did you have a microfilming system in the archives, microfilming of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I came to the archive on the 13th of July, 1999. It was after the war, after the bombing. Microfiche documents exist, they had been put on microfiche before. As far as I know it wasn't possible to microfilm documents after 1999 because the laboratory and the equipment had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, the next question for my own understanding is: Who set the criteria, the standard, for putting documents in the archives? I mean, did somebody check the criteria or any document would come? And then the second aspect would be: What system existed for inspection of the documents by anybody who would like to have access to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who set the criteria? When it comes to documents, I don't know that. As for the second part of your question, I didn't quite understand it. Did you have in mind how documents can be used or what? I'm sorry, I didn't understand the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I need a document -- I just want to see a document, I go to the archives or whosoever is in charge. What am I to do to make a formal request that I want to see a document and then how would that be inspected? Did you allow somebody to take the pen inside or only a pencil which could be rubbered off or could he take pictures or could he copy it? What happened? I mean, how did you preserve the document after it was given over to somebody for inspection? I mean, how was that done? Who was overseeing what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood it now. In the military archive there are collections which contain open material, and that material is open for all researchers. In that case persons who are citizens of Serbia need just come in and submit a request to the chief of the military archive and write the topic that they want to research. Then the chief of the military archive would either authorise them or not authorise them. And following that they would receive the documents that they could review. In the reading room where the documents are normally inspected, there mustn't be - at least that's how it used to be - any cameras, all cameras are prohibited, as is all additional equipment. The desks had to be without drawers, and the bags that researchers brought with them had to be kept separately. And there was always a custodian present in the reading room to assist and to supervise. This pertains to the open archive material. When it comes to foreign citizens, then a request needs to be made through an embassy or through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. At any rate, the request is submitted through the appropriate embassy. When it comes to collections containing closed material, there is the material that has not been put in right order, and that is of classified nature. There is a special procedure for accessing those documents, but unfortunately I'm not very familiar with this field because I worked in the department for open, non-classified material, and the procedure there was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I wonder if you can answer this question, but after how long, after what passage of time, a classified material became unclassified and open? Was there a system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is done identically at the level of all archives in the world. As far as I know, there is a set period of time that needs to pass before material is opened up for research. Until that is done, the material needs to be put in order and prepared in order to be made available to the researchers. That's all that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, you described how there were -- there was one original and then I think there were three copies made of this inventory that's in Exhibit 3D1130.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have that on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that right, there are three copies made in addition to the one original?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in principle there were three copies in total. And when necessary, when an independent unit needed it, then a fourth copy would be produced; but in principle, there existed only three copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were the copies made with a colour copier or is it a black-and-white copy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could observe, they were all black and white. You know, while we used typewriters one could see that a copy is made through a carbon paper. But when we improved the equipment, I think that people made one copy and then made copies based on that or they saved it as an original and then made additional copies; but I'm not fully familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is the copy we have on the screen now we can see the stamp in the upper left-hand corner is red with some blue ink writing, and the handwritten changes you told us you made and the totals appear to be in blue ink. So that leads me to wonder: Is this the original or is this a colour copy of the original?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at this I would say that this is the original, but this is by no means certain because when three copies are produced these identical stamps can be placed on all three of them and numbers entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the handwriting in blue ink would only be on the original and the copies would appear in black, as in a photocopy; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, we had three archive lists. We weren't allowed to copy them. We weren't allowed to do it in any other way. After correcting the first copy, we had to correct the second and the third copy. So basically all of them had blue ink, which means that there was no photocopying. We were not allowed to photocopy this because this was not our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I think I understand. So in essence you made three originals at the same time with the handwritten changes on each of the three copies; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on how this was done, yes. But, for example, if the person preparing the lists, he may have made one as the original and then the authorised officer signed the original and then second and third copy were the photocopies. So when we corrected something, then they were all considered originals; but when things were signed, it's possible that the person signing signed just the first copy and the second and third were photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as the handwritten changes you made, did you make them on three separate copies, or did you make them on one copy and then photocopy that one that you had made handwritten changes on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would first do it on the one copy, we would make corrections and check the document. Once we were done with the first one, then we would take the second one and do the same and then the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so you made handwriting on a second copy and a third copy where you filled in the number of documents and the number of leaves in your own handwriting, in blue ink?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's answered that twice, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. So if this one entry that you told us you did not make was made by another individual at a later date, wouldn't we be able to understand that by obtaining the other two copies to see if the same change had been made on those two?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to see all copies. Perhaps it is visible there, but I don't know it right now. I don't know whether it was done on all copies or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be that we have one of them, which is 3D1108.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an explanation for this, for why there is a stamp in the upper corner. The explanation is of a technical nature, but I can do it later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can deal with it in re-examination I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this is a question that should be put to the witness. It's a matter of technical nature explaining how the documents are provided by the government to the Tribunal, and the witness doesn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can hear that later. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this document in the upper left-hand corner where we have a stamp from the Supreme Command Staff, could you read that number for me? It's a confidential number and the date is the 10th of August. Could you read the number that's on that original?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 400-6, if I can see this well on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's been translated in the English version as 100-K. I think if we look at 3D1108 you'll see that copy, the quality I guess is so much different that I can understand how the number on 1108 might have gotten translated as 100-K instead of 400-6. I think you see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, I don't have another question for you about that. But I did want to ask you, in terms of when people are in the reading room in the archive, is there some kind of log or guest book or register kept of who came to look at documents and which documents they looked at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you as far as the department where I was an administrator, there are full records concerning the open material kept there about persons who worked in the reading room. It is normally recorded exactly what documents they inspected, what they photocopied, what was issued to them, and so on. As for the other department, I don't know since I didn't work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I notice the date in the stamp in the left-hand corner from the Supreme Command Staff is the 10th of August and then the date I guess that you checked this group of documents in is the 24th of September, 1999. Do you know any reason why there was a six-week difference? Was it just typed up and it took them six weeks to bring it to you, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question yesterday when Defence counsel asked me what I thought about the time-period between the 10th of August and the 24th. Should I repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, because I didn't hear it or I forget.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I explained yesterday, when the list was prepared and when all the bundles were packed up, loaded on a truck, because there was a lot of material and it was mostly brought in by trucks, most likely they needed to load it up and to come to the location where we were housed and then it needed to be unloaded there and then it needed to be put in right order before we proceeded with inspecting and receiving these documents. Physically it was impossible to inspect the amount of material that was brought in. Physically it was impossible. Most likely this is why there is this situation with the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it it's not unusual for there to be a gap of time between the date it's typed up and the time that you receive it, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness started working in the archive after the war and this seemed to be an exceptional situation where there were piles of documents which had been compiled during the war which had to be dealt with as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This wasn't a routine situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct or is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. Because if you were to receive a large number of documents, you would need a certain amount of time to go over it, to prepare it. So it's very similar. One couldn't do it from one day to the next one, and this is not something that can be done in haste. It needs to be done properly because it is retained permanently and there shouldn't be any mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last topic I wanted to ask you about at page 18, line 20, Mr. Ackerman asked you about a possibility of Milorad [sic] Jankovic who typed up this list, if in doing that he realized he had made a mistake and perhaps made that handwritten change and wrote in 248-2 and changed the number from 1 and 3 to 2 and 5 before he brought it to you. Wouldn't you have noticed that there was a handwritten change made by somebody before it reached you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, his name is Miodrag. I think that you used another first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is this: Had he corrected it, this would have been taken into account when adding up documents and leaves on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if he had made that change where he had entered the handwritten entry below the number instead of above, would you have changed that and moved it to above the typewritten number in accordance with your standard procedures?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that if he had entered the correction, he should have initialled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you had seen some corrections on there, when you received it you would have asked him to put his initials on it, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had not initialled it, I would have told my immediate superior, then he would have taken action. But if he corrected it and didn't initial it, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, could you complete that answer. In fact, answer that again, please. What you -- what's been recorded here doesn't make sense. The question is: Would you have asked him to put his initials beside any correction he had made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that if I were to come across such a situation where it was entered in this way and that there were no initials indicating who had made the correction, then I would have given it to my immediate supervisor for him to take appropriate action. And if there were initials indicating who had made the correction, then I would have accepted it; and if there were no initials, I would have given it to my superior, because our superiors were there to handle situations of this nature, a situation where things were unclear to us and where we didn't know how to proceed, they would take over then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you had a document like this where the changes were made below the number instead of above the number by someone else other than you, you wouldn't have let that go through, would you, because you know your bosses would have complained to you about not following procedure; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, that's a meaningless question, Mr. Hannis, with all due respect, because what matters is the initial. So let's ask the question on the basis that the number is below and is initialled, if you think there's any point in asking that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'll stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Visnjic, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see in e-court the same exhibit, that is to say the one we see now, and would it be possible to see pages 7 and 8 in B/C/S on the screen simultaneously? On the left half could we zoom in to row 82, especially the figures in that row. A bit more, a bit more. This is fine. And then on the right side we need the following page, page 9. I apologise. [In English] Right, the last page, the last page on the right side -- oh, then down. I'm sorry. Then [Interpretation] scroll down, please, towards the bottom, we need the signature in the left corner. Could we enlarge the signature as much as possible. A bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Mladenovski, in your career how many times did it happen that one person made corrections in one type of pencil and then takes a fountain pen and signs it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened often, especially when it comes to signing because it's much nicer to sign in a fountain pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked you whether you worked under pressure and how much time you needed to do the archive lists, and you started giving an answer on page 15. And you said that you worked on this type of material from 1999. Can you tell us how long was this material worked on? You said from 1999 until it was time to move into the building.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been late 2000 or early 2001, when the building was ready to be moved in. It could have been June or July 2001 that we moved into the building, the building that had been renovated. Naturally we had to make preparations to move everything that had been placed elsewhere, to put it back into the building, to pack everything so that the archive could work properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, it could have been at least a year and a half to two years?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that. And as for us working under pressure, I said that we didn't. Nobody really drove us to work --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Mr. Ackerman asked you about the possibility of having some person, let's say Miodrag Jankovic, making a correction of the document before the document reached you. The Prosecutor asked you the same thing. I'm asking you this now: Based on what you said today, when could a correction in the archive list be made at the earliest?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The earliest it could have been made was after the 24th of September, that is to say the 25th of September, 1999. Theoretically the latest it could have been done was until the date the archive list was photocopied, but I'm saying theoretically that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am not understanding that, I'm afraid. This is between -- the date you've got is between the arrival in the office, is it? I think I'm now not understanding what the relevance of the 24th of September is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood based on what the witness said, Your Honours, the correction in row 82 could have been done after the 24th of September until today, until the photocopy was made, not before the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So what I've now not understood is the significance of the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look on page 1 when this archive list was made up, if you look at the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand the idea, but it's what the relevance of the 24th of September is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the day when the inspection was made and the archive list was signed, where there was no correction in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The day it's signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, who signed this archive list on the 24th of September, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how could an alteration be made after that date? I'm sorry, it must be my stupidity, but I'm not understanding how after the 24th - where is your question? - your question was: When could -- make a correction before the document reached the witness. "When could a correction in the archive list be made by Jankovic?" And the answer is: After the 24th. Now, I have to say, Mr. Visnjic, I do not understand that. I thought that was impossible on what we've been told so far. So please try to help me or explain where I'm being stupid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question may have been a rhetorical one. What we are claiming is that after the 24th of September, 1999, which includes the imaginary Miodrag Jankovic, somebody entered a correction in the archive list without authorisation to do so, and that could have been done between the 24th of September and the day when the photocopy arrived at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not the question in English, so it may be a translation difficulty. The question was: "Mr. Ackerman asked you about the possibility of having some person, let's say Jankovic, making a correction of the document before it reached you. The Prosecutor asked you the same thing. I'm asking you this now: Based on what you said today, when could a correction in the archive list be made at the earliest?" I assumed that question related to the same issue, but you're saying it relates to a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's more a conclusion than fact so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Are you going to be much longer because we'll run out of -- we're already well past the break and we'll run out of -- it would be nice to finish with the witness and I thought that's what you were trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would help not to complicate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the witness to be shown 3D1131, page 2, and could we show column 248, the B/C/S version will suffice, the right-hand side. Could we have the right-hand corner of row 248, a bit more. A bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovski, do you see the stamp in red ink in column number 9, line 248?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not very clear, but it looks like the 31st of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little bit. A bit more, please. Thank you. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please scroll up a little bit or down, down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 31st of July, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what does it say next to that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says keep permanently, military archives, inventory number 21606/99 and there are initials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what in your view this date represents, the 31st of July, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume this should be the date to the best of my recollection in the log-book. That's when the document is handed over to the person in charge of archiving the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we take another look at 3D1130, please, page 5. Could we look at number 5 in the B/C/S version, correction where the number 5 has been entered. [In English] Yes. Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we have IC197, please -- 5, sorry. Mr. Mladenovski, have you ever used an electronic pen to write on glass?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MLADENOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Could I give you my explanation after the break in connection with the stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mladenovski, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall take the break now and resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment. I don't want interrupt and I hesitate doing this, but what Mr. Visnjic is fixing to explain to you all is of evidentiary significance, then I think it's improper for him to be explaining it, it should come from a witness. But I leave that judgement to your wisdom, Your Honour. I think it's evidentiary significance, but you're a better judge of that than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I should continue. I only want you to look at some documents which we received from the Government of Serbia where you will see the differences and why the differences are there. I don't know whether we need the witness because these documents do not concern the witness and his testimony. I can explain to you what the procedure is when documents are obtained from the Government of Serbia, and then it's up to you to draw a conclusion from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The stamp you're now showing on the left-hand side of the screen looks like the same stamp as was on the top right-hand corner of one of the copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honours. When you receive documents from the Government of Serbia, the archive certifies every copy leaving the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you stole the unstamped one, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. For forensic reasons we asked to get a special photocopy, and you can see that in Exhibit 1134 when for forensic reasons we asked for the photocopy to be in colour and without any markings so that it can be used for an expert report. We asked for the document which looks just as it looks in the archives, without any stamps, extra stamps on it. And I can show you on the example we have before us, this is the log-book of the office of the Chief of the General Staff and there's one copy with a stamp and one without it. There are two log -- there's -- this is a whole log-book and you can't have two documents, one with a stamp and one without. And you'll see that two months ago we received this document without a stamp, and the ones we received before were certified with a stamp as evidence that the documents reached us directly from the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is this another one you asked for especially for your forensic science purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours, and we explained all this in our submission of the 29th of February, 2008, in paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where we specified in detail what we requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Zecevic, is it now your turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness, the joint expert witness, Mr. -- Professor Branimir Jokic, but maybe before the witness comes in we have the issue with the -- our motion for -- to amend the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry that we -- that we filed this motion this late, and I understand the problem that Mr. Hannis is having. But, Your Honours, in all honesty, we tried -- I tried myself to understand this report which is more than 1600 pages now -- with all annexes. Now, Your Honours, when -- during the proofing I insisted with the expert that he gives me the concrete examples because that was the only way how I would probably understand his position taken in report. Now when he -- to my satisfaction explained me the -- on the concrete examples, I then decided that it is probably the best way to present and to -- to present his expert report in court and to be able to assist all the parties -- to all the parties in understanding this relatively, at least for me relatively complicated science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And -- yeah, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's try to get this in some sort of perspective. Mr. Hannis, the only averments in this indictment about buildings in the cultural sense relate to mosques. 77(d) is the only place I can find any reference to damage to cultural structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So mosques only?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we've got this elaborate report about Kulas and town centres and so on, but that doesn't seem to feature in any aspect of the indictment. So we're not letting -- going to let this grow arms and legs at this stage on the basis of a report going to over a thousand pages about an issue that doesn't exist if we're -- there's no point in shadow boxing around this, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that there has been evidence about Kulas. I can't find any oral evidence about anything else beyond that apart from mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Riedlmayer talked about perhaps a library and archive, but they're mostly related to the mosque or Islamic religious buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think there was talk about the old town in Djakovica as well, old town centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there actually oral evidence about that or is it confined to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he spoke about that when looking at one of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where is your averment that's got anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps it only relates to the general averment about persecutions on religious grounds and ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a number of these exhibits proposed do relate to mosques or Orthodox places of worship, and therefore are potentially relevant. I take it there's been some effort made to try to reach agreement on this, but that has foundered, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll tell you from my point of view it was -- I didn't realize until looking at the list, and I'm talking about Exhibits I think 1D777 through 799. 799 is the one that I just received at 1.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a photograph of some monument in Landovica, I think. And just looking at what they are I'm not sure how that fits into the evidence. That's what makes me uncomfortable. I haven't had time to talk to Mr. Zecevic and say what do you want this for, perhaps we could have resolved this. But now at this late stage, this is an expert, and it just seems like it's the kind of thing that I shouldn't have to get last-minute notice of when I'm trying to deal with a report that includes with 1600 pages, et cetera. I do not have an objection to 1D796, which is a CV of Andrew Herscher, which you might understand why I have no objection to. It's in English, I know who he is, and I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about 1D797 which relates to something you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object to that if that's the statement of Mr. Ilic concerning a photograph he took in the presence or nonpresence of UN troops on the 13th of June. That's a statement of a witness outside of court. If that doesn't comply with the requirements of Rule 92 and I don't think it should be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it you won't be relying on the account of what Mr. Riedlmayer gives of what Mr. Ilic had to say in that event because it did seem to be part of the basis for the suggestion that there was Serb involvement in the damage to this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
