utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I take issue with the part of Mr. Ilic's statement that there were no Serb police. I'm not sure -- I don't have the statement in front of me at the moment. I may be mistaking that with what Mr. Jokic says in his report, suggesting that there were no Serb police present in the city on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Zecevic, just one other matter. The only charge to which this can be relevant is a charge under Article 5 of the Statute, a crime against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the report's been written very much as if it was dealing with a war crime allegation under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I -- well, I do agree with Your Honour, but the concept of the report was actually like -- like an answer to Riedlmayer and Herscher report, and it is actually named evaluation of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. But it's not been presented as a report supporting a charge under Article 3. However, turning to your documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may give another comment on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, basically all the documents that Mr. Hannis is actually referring to, which he has a problem -- and which are definitely relevant have been included because of my endeavour to present to you on a -- on examples in court because I think that would be the most effective. On the other hand, all the data contained in these documents is already a part of the report. It is all part of the annex 5 of the report which is the MNEMOSYNE report from 2001, and I can give my friend, Mr. Hannis, relevant pages. I just -- based on these facts I thought that this is not going to be an issue between us and our friends from Prosecutor's side because these are just the documents on which -- of which contents -- contents of which are already in the report -- a part of the report, so these are just actual documents. And I can provide the relevant pages right now if you want me to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We take the view that it's too late now to tender documents about which there is contention where the Prosecutor is unable because of lack of time to prepare himself adequately to deal with them, and therefore the only one we will add to the 65 ter list is 1D796, which is by agreement of the parties. The others will not be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One other matter, if I may. We found an objection to the report and ask that this witness be called for cross-examine. I do have an issue with about six of the annexes, and I don't know if you want to me to address that now or after you've heard from the witnesses on direct, but they have to do with the position that most of them go to post-war destruction, and therefore I don't think they're relevant. One of them is listed as a draft document on its face and is missing 25 pages in the middle; so I have some concerns about that. I don't know if you want to hear that now or at the end of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we'll deal with the admission of annexes to this report once we've heard the evidence, but it's by no means a foregone conclusion that all these annexes will be thought by us to be of probative value in the context of the case. There's no doubt they're retaliate, but what probative value they have is the real issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we now have the witness, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Jokic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we intended to give you a binder of documents in the courtroom for you to use in the course of your testimony, but by a decision of the Trial Chamber we are unable to use these documents. So I will put questions to you based on your expert report. Do you have your expert report with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: With me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I have it in my hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have just one minute, Your Honour, to organize --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an extra copy in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, thank you. We're very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, please take a look and tell us whether this is the report compiled by you, and here it's marked 1D743.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I hope it is because I can't look at all of it right now, but yes it looks like that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the report on the monitor. Do you see it on the monitor, Professor?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's easier for me to look at the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the last page, leaf through it, look at some features that will enable you to identify it so that we can tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to move to little closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence that's it. Maybe some photographs are missing, which I had included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the photographs, at the end of the report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have that particular page on the screen, please, it is page -- it is page 37.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found the photographs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise, the two pages were stuck together. I found them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, is this your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you accept it as yours. Do you have anything to add or change perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add, and through your questions probably I will touch on everything that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Professor, would you add anything to the text itself?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have 1D743 without the annexes admitted as report as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no problem with that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Jokic, within the scope of your report is your CV, and from it it's evident that between 1998 and 1999 you were the director of the museum in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, in that period, I was the director of the museum in Pristina, which I still am but now in the Displaced Museum with its headquarters in Belgrade. That's it's official title now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm pausing for the interpretation, just so you know. Mr. Jokic, can you tell us how many Albanians were employed in the museum between 1998 and 1999 while you were the director in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: At the time I was appointed director of the museum in Pristina, the situation I found was the following: The ethnic breakdown of the employees was approximately equal. If one looks at the numbers of Serbs, Albanians, Turks, Roma, and other ethnicities, it was an exemplary team if one looks at inter-ethnic relations and professional attitudes to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But my question was how many Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: About 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the Serbian ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were 13 members of the Serbian ethnic groups I think and then there were also Roma, Turks, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Fatmir Peja mean anything to you; and if so, can you tell us what duty this gentleman performed in the museum while you were the director?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fatmir Peja is a colleague of mine, he was the custodian -- he was the curator, that is, and he was in charge of numismatics. We had excellent working relations and excellent communication and we still do to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As it is not -- has not entered the transcript, what was his duty in the museum?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: He was the curator, that was his profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in the bodies of management?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the management board, which is the highest-ranking organ of management in an organization, in an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kemal Ljuci, what can you tell me about him, was he employed there while you were the director? What do you know about him after you left Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Kemal Ljuci was also a curator, he was an archaeologist. He was one of the most active employees, and professionally he cooperated with all archaeologists from the territory of the Republic of Serbia. In 1998 in the -- at the Assembly -- at the gathering of archaeologists of Serbia in Subotica he presided. He --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the end of that answer, please, the interpreter didn't catch it. It might be an idea if you come closer to the microphone, please, so that everything is heard. But you told us that in 1998 at the gathering of archaeologists of Serbia in Subotica he presided, and then you said something else which the interpreter did not hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He presided at the assembly of archaeologists of Serbia, and at the exhibition which was held at the Gallery of the Serbian Academy of Sciences in Belgrade, he was a commissioner of that exhibition, which means that he was the main expert in charge of implementing and organizing the exhibition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when was this exhibition held, the one that you mention, where he was a commissioner of the exhibition?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: That exhibition was held in February of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade in the gallery of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last name we have here, Xhafer Lokaj, that person is mentioned by Mr. Riedlmayer and Mr. Herscher in their report. What can you tell us about Xhafer Lokaj first of all, was he employed at the museum and then everything else that's relevant? Please keep it at a slow pace for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Xhafer Lokaj was employed in the provincial institute for the protection of monuments in Pristina. He worked there as a person in charge of preserving -- preservationist, and he was also a contract worker of the museum in Pristina. I personally hired him to perform certain tasks based on his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lokaj and the fact that he was of a certain profession and that he worked at the museum, was he familiar with the documents of the museum, with its standards, with the methodology that was used at the museum and at the institute for preservation -- for protection of monuments in Pristina, where he worked?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that Mr. Xhafer Lokaj was a very well-respected painter and preservationist. He restored frescos in many monasteries in Kosovo and Metohija. Given that he worked in that field for some 20 years, everything that concerns the methodology of work and standards on which the preservation work is based and given his long-term experience in this field, based on all of that I believe that he was well familiar with everything in the field of methodology and standards when it comes to protection of cultural property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 56-30 of your report, or rather, page 30, item 6-30, there is a statement given by you which stems from the UNESCO report which is annex to your opinion, to your expert opinion, where it says that allegedly the Albanians didn't hold high positions and responsible positions in the institutions aimed at preserving cultural property in Kosovo from 1990 to about 1999. Can you tell us what your opinion is about this claim?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we find that in English, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 5.6-30 -- page 30, it is in the column called arguments, arguments, and I believe it's the third paragraph from the end. It starts with: "The Albanians ..." 5.6-30 -- it is the page 29 in e-court, and it starts after the [indiscernible] the Albanians with the word Albanians, argumentation column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it the page that's now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So the ultimate column to the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- called argumentation, halfway down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Professor, please give us a reply if you remember the question.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I remember the question but it's difficult to me -- for me to orient myself in the document because it has both English and Serbian. These are arbitrary conclusions and I will tell you why. There is no overall insight into the situation in various institutions. This amounts to various research projects, one of which was performed by representative of UNESCO, Mr. Borath. Based on that we can conclude what the national composition or ethnic composition was in various institutions from 1975 until 1999. If the Trial Chamber is interested, I can give you details, I can elaborate on this, but only if you think that that would be of assistance; if not, I will just stand by my earlier answer, namely, that such a statement is not fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you wish to say that -- let us now focus on 1998 and 1999, when you were there personally. Are you trying to say that the Albanians held responsible positions in the institutions dealing with culture in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: They did hold responsible positions. When it comes to leading positions, the situation there is somewhat different. It's a process, as I have said to you, that lasted for a number of years, from 1975 until 1990 the dominant, leading staff was made up of Albanians; however, then certain changes came about and the political situation was what it was and changes were implemented. As for the nature of those changes, I don't know if it's up to me to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please tell me, was there an institute for Albanology in Pristina and who led that institute?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: There certainly was the institute for Albanology and it was natural for such an institute to be led by an Albanian. It's quite a natural thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us now turn to a different topic. Tell me, please, do you know when the first law on cultural property for the territory of the entire Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted? We don't need the exact date, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, in the archives, in the documentation, we see years 1952, 1954, both years figure due to the procedure that was in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on that law, Professor, the institute for protection of cultural and historical monuments was established in the territory of each republic and province including Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. All of the republics had their own laws and institutes. They had their own services dealing with the protection of cultural heritage. In 1977 the institutions for protecting cultural property were joined at the level of Yugoslavia. The entire system of protection of cultural property was based on that principle until the competencies were divided again and until it was placed under the jurisdiction of each republic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The other law that regulated this field was adopted in 1977; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that law was adopted in 1977, and that is the year when for the first time in the service for protection of cultural monuments the cultural monuments were classified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "classified," do you mean that they were categorized?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were categorized. There existed three categories in protecting monuments. One was a monument, one was a monument of great importance, and the third one was monument of exceptional importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, and then there was a law that was passed in 1994 about cultural property?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, there was the law that was passed in 1994 as well, and it was amended to a certain extent but that did not affect the system of protection of cultural heritage in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was amended to a certain extent, do you mean to say that in 1994 the law that was passed in 1994 amended to some extent the law from 1977 but that did not affect the system of protection of cultural property. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: When I said that it did not affect the system, I meant it did not adversely affect the system. And there was a positive influence because that system of protection of cultural heritage was improved and that amendment included the improvements as specified by UNESCO and other institutions. All laws are amended in order to be improved and kept in line with the standards at the global level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, very briefly, the regulations from 1994 as well as the law from 1977, does this legislation accept the standards that are in place in UNESCO and is it in compliance with the rules of profession with professional standards. Do these laws, in fact, implement these principles?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they absolutely do and that was done at the level of the entire Yugoslavia. The system of protection was the same, there was no difference in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This law from 1994, does it regulate what is a cultural and historical property? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does define it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The law from 1994, does it envisage an identical criterion for all monuments regardless of their provenance, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Monuments were not discriminated against regardless of their provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this law also set forth the method of establishing how a certain facility or a certain site is declared to be a cultural and historical property?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this law also envisage a register or the register of cultural and historical properties in the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like any other law because this is unavoidable, we need the register of cultural property, it's an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this law also set forth some sort of supervision, a supervision mechanism by a ministry; and if so, which ministry if the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the implementation of this law is in the hands of the appropriate ministry, Ministry of Culture in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, annex 8 of your report is, in fact, a bulletin of statistics from the 31st of December, 1994, where all immovable cultural property is registered. Could we please see annex 8 which is page 1.123 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Annex 8, page 1.123, Exhibit 1D743. [In English] If the Court would permit me, I would like to give to the witness -- could we hand him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you the original so that it's easier for you to follow.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it page 1. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1.123 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's the same in both B/C/S and English, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is in B/C/S, Your Honour. It is -- I'm informed here that -- let me consult, Your Honour, just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What we can provide at this point is the ID number, it's 1D09-1643. You have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, please tell me, what is the total number of registered cultural property according to the statistical bulletin of the Republic of Serbia dated the 31st of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Up until the time the statistics were compiled, the number of cultural properties in Kosovo was 410.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Out of this total number, how many registered cultural properties were of Islamic provenance?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Islamic provenance, 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer in their report speak of 15 allegedly protected monuments of Islamic provenance in Kosovo and you give us the figure of 91. Who's correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not me, it's the statistics that's correct. It's not about me. I don't think that they could give you that number and that it was correct because I don't think that Mr. Herscher had insight into the entire number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how many monuments there are of Orthodox provenance according to the statistics -- to the statistical bulletin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the rest that make up the total of 410?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: 168 cultural properties were of general importance, those were bridges, bazaars, and other types of monuments, monuments from Second World War and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Tell me, please, according to your records, according to your knowledge, how many are there unregistered immovables cultural properties of Orthodox provenance in Kosovo, meaning the ones that were not included in this list because they were of a lesser importance or there was some other reason?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: There are over 1.000 such sites of religious character.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, please tell me, in relation to the total number, how many unregistered -- or rather, registered cultural properties in that bulletin originate from the 20th century, do they represent a minority or a majority?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: The number is small. I will tell you exactly. When it comes to the 20th century -- so when it comes to monuments of Christian or Serbian provenance in the 20th century, the ones that originate from the 20th century, none of them were declared a cultural property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the monuments of Islamic provenance that were created in the 20th century, are some of them included in that list; and if so, which ones are they, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: In this list there are just two monuments of Islamic provenance that were declared cultural property and that were created between 1901 and 1913, and those are imperial mosque in Pristina and Ati [phoen] mosque in Gnjilane. This is something that contradicts, that denies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, in the list, or rather, pursuant to the decision of the Government of the Republic of Serbia just two religious sites from the 20th century were included in the list of protected cultural properties, and both of them are of Islamic provenance; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and they were declared so in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 5215 -- or rather, page 15, 5.2 of your report, which is page 15 in English, e-court, of your report, which is 1D743. There you responded to the claims of Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher - I'm going to paraphrase - that the protocols -- Hague Protocols to the Geneva Conventions from 1949, that they make it necessary to use the cultural standards in declaring a facility to be -- have you found that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't need to find that. I know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely agree. A broader interpretation of conventions only lead to improvement of the system of protection and assessment, and the existing standards can only be improved in that way, they cannot be disqualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please -- tell me, please, according to you what would serve as a standard for categorizing a religious facility? The -- let me see if I can enumerate this. Would it be as -- would it be a criterion that it's a facility or an area where a religious service is performed, would that be a criterion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think 62, 2, I said would it be a facility or an area where religious service is performed. Secondly, according to you, would it necessarily serve as a feature of a religious facility the fact that that facility is so declared by the religious community to which it belongs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and say are those the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I understand -- I accept that. I actually -- I said that I would try to speed the things up, that's why I wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that we have the Prosecution position then perhaps you would ask open questions, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, according to you what else is a feature, basic feature, of a religious facility?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the main feature of a religious facility is that it needs to be so declared by a religious community, Islamic community in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The religious community to which it belongs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the head, the leader, or the religious official at the head of that religious facility also needs to be accepted and recognised by the religious community to which he belongs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Every religious community has its own hierarchy and the manner in which it functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a law regulating the status of religious communities and religious buildings so that religious ceremonies can take place and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at republican level there is a law regulating the work of religious communities without drawing any distinctions between the origin of these communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it perhaps the law on the legal status of religious communities?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware, Professor, of whether that law envisages the existence of approval by appropriate municipal organs for a religious building to be declared as such and for religious rights to be carried out in it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Like every other building, a building of religious character has to go through a certain procedure and get approval from certain organs at the municipal level and it acquires the attribute of religious building by a decision of the religious community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'll take you back to your report, page 5, paragraph 5, page 21, that's page 20 in e-court in English, and 1D743 again, where you stated the selection Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher based their conclusions on in their report. To avoid repetition -- to avoid repeating what is already in your report, let me just remind you that there was mention of ethnic colouring of sources and also you criticized the statement by Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher that local teams carried out observations and assisted them in compiling this report. That's on page -- the page before this, 54 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question of the Professor. Can you name for us any mosque -- or rather, any building with a minaret that looks like a mosque which you say is not approved for religious purposes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I included in my report what was available to me from the documentation. I would not like to make an evaluation if I cannot support it with facts. I suggested that certain documents be presented, and I hope that they're at your disposal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, we've limited time in this institution to deal with this and there's a handful of mosques mentioned in the indictment and we're going to spend an interminable length of time going through records and statistics for some elusive feature. You know, if it's called a cat and looks like a cat, it's likely to be a cat. So can you help me on your experience of Kosovo whether mosque-like structures tended not to be properly authorised for religious purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only tell you what is in the documentation and what I can confirm. There is a mosque in Dobrivo, in Peduha, if you look at this you will see that these are the mosques in question, in Dzabari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean these are the mosques in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the fact that I was unable to get proper documentation to confirm that these are really religious buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's time for our break. We have to break at this stage for half an hour, Professor. While we have that break, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we start I would just -- I talked to my friend Mr. Hannis. We would like to substitute with the Serbian copy, the whole Serbian copy, of the expert report and give it to the witness. Because he -- thank you very much. It's already with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the usher will now hand you a full version of your report in the Serbian language to make things easier for you, to make it easier for you to follow, that is.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a small digression. Judge Bonomy asked you a little while ago, just before the break, Professor in your opinion in a hypothetical situation if in some area of Serbia where there is no strict town planning in place I were to build a residential building resembling a church in architecture with domes, for example, and placed a cross on it, would it be a religious building in your view or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to say. We probably didn't understand one another very well. I didn't say in advance whether something can or cannot be a religious building, that would not be very serious on my part. But if one wants to give an expert opinion, one has to have the prerequisites, the basic prerequisites for a religious building in view of the nature of its architecture, it has to have the proper documentation in order to be identified as a religious or cultural building, it has to be recognised as such by the state; otherwise, there's no other way we can tell that's what it is. And this gives rise to confusion because churches all follow the same architectural design, for example. So out of a hundred churches or buildings, if one doesn't have the appropriate documentation we can't really tell what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're the person who's done the research and we would like to know if you've come across any example of a building that looks like a church but isn't one. You can't come here as an expert and hide behind the law and say, Well, I don't know because I haven't had access to the documents. That doesn't help us in the least. We need to know what conclusions and opinions you as an expert have formed about whether there are buildings in Kosovo which look like mosques but are not according to the law. Now, that would help us if you could tell us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did my expert opinion on the documentation and the report of Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher. I was not tasked with carrying out investigations in the field. I compiled my report based on the documentation I was given and it is confusing. I cannot state an opinion on something for which I have no parameters. Where the parameters exist I offered the documentation from the land registry books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may help in some instances. As far as the law is concerned then lawyers can present the law to us in advance of their arguments and we can make an assessment of the situation whether we accept that -- if the law requires certain procedure and it has not been complied with then the building is not a religious building. But we don't need a professor from a museum to tell us about the law on the matter. We can read that and draw our own conclusions. We thought you would be coming to tell us something about the existence of apparently religious buildings which aren't religious buildings, but it doesn't look as though we're going to have that assistance so let's proceed with what we can hear from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, I would only say that Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher conducted -- had they compiled their report as the service requires, it would have been supported by the proper documents. I can tell you what sort of documents are needed for a religious or cultural property to be identified as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your report tells us that as I understand it. But, you see, this indictment refers to specific places. Now, it refers to mosques in 1, 2 -- I think 14 municipalities and it would be of interest to hear from you if you had an opinion about whether these were mosques or not. If you're not in a position to tell us that, then we can move on to other things that Mr. Zecevic wants to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can be of assistance, Your Honours, there is a part where we are talking about the concrete examples, that is why I wanted to present these exhibits in order to facilitate that. But in any case, it would take us a bit longer but we will get there definitely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll have your two hours, Mr. Zecevic. At the moment we're not persuaded that this investigation requires longer. If by the end of it we're making some progress on something really material, then the position may be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we started talking about the selection of sources, the sources used by Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer. You spoke about this on page 18 of your report, they referred to local teams. Do you have a brief comment to make as our time is limited, as you have heard?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I do have a comment on this. In view of my experience and my work on the protection of the cultural heritage, I don't see that there was a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in your opinion, including you as an expert, is it possible to identify a building if you are not familiar with it, it hasn't been described in the literature, and you're not familiar with the location, could you identify such a building?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, the -- it's not just me but the protection service doesn't work that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that professional practice requires that these buildings be presented in such a way that an expert can identify them, do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Every religious property and cultural property has its documentation which is published and is available to the professional -- to the profession of large -- at large. So any service dealing with protection of such buildings has to have at its disposal the documentation pertaining to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But if we were to discuss buildings not on the list, not protected as immovable cultural goods, if they are simply religious buildings, in that case is some sort of identification necessary or is it sufficient for someone to tell you something about such a building or draw your attention to it? Would you accept that as evidence for you to be able to identify the building?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't be according to my will, but according to the rules of the service every such building, whether religious or non-religious, has to have a licence in order to be used, it has to have its plans, the plans for its building, and this also applies to civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does your profession require verification of certain data or not when conducting the sort of investigation Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer conducted?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Certainly, that has to be done. Before you set out on a trip you have to know what building you're going to visit, you have to have certain technical documentation on the basis of which you can identify the building on the ground; without that, it's impossible to establish, it's absolutely impossible to establish the identity of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you calculated in your report on page 22 how much time Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer spent in the field, in Kosovo, and you related this to the number of buildings they described. Can you give me some information about this, and in your view how much time would be needed for a correct, well-founded professional report to be compiled?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: I can give you my opinion based on my personal experience and the experience of my colleagues. It's impossible to visit -- it's physically impossible to visit this number of buildings in that time, especially if we know that the terrain in Kosovo and Metohija is what it is and what the roads are like. It's impossible to reach all these buildings in that amount of time. It's even impossible to prepare the technical and expert documentation to go out on the field because you can't put your hands in your pocket and go out on the ground because you can't identify a building. We know what sort of problems we faced when we went looking for a building in the field on the ground, we lost hours looking for the building. So probably Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer were in a difficult situation and I understand what situation they were in. It wasn't easy for them to cope with that problem and they probably didn't have the proper associates who could help them carry out their work faster and more expeditiously and more thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, bearing in mind that Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher described 230 buildings throughout Kosovo and Metohija, tell me, in your professional practice and according to what you know, how much time would be needed for an optimal investigation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for that question. Identifying 230 buildings throughout Kosovo, maybe 200 of them are all in Pristina. It's vague, it's -- I don't think it's something that can be answered without some further elaboration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's already been answered in the report as I understand it. We've got a time --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not say he spent less than an hour investigating each one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is it exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do we need to ask him again? You just get an objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you participated in the MNEMOSYNE project?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, that project had a task broader than the project engaged in by Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many experts of various sorts were included in that project?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, to carry out this project in a professional and qualified way you needed at least five or six experts, an architect -- that was the number of experts needed and you needed a professional photographer, that was very important because no amateur photograph can be used to identify a building. Whoever has engaged in such work can confirm this. If that was the way buildings could be identified, then you wouldn't need to have a professional photographer with you, that wouldn't be a condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many teams of experts did you have at your disposal when working on the MNEMOSYNE project?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: We had four teams which changed, one worked in the morning, one in the afternoon, and we were barely able to visit the area of Metohija in almost six months. So to visit almost -- to visit all of Kosovo and Metohija properly you would need at least a year to work on all these buildings. Someone might find this strange, but I'll tell you that this is exhausting work and very demanding work if you want to do everything that the protection of such buildings requires to give a proper opinion, a professional opinion, on a cultural or religious building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly - and just answer with a yes or no answer - you had about 30 experts at your disposal and four teams worked in parallel and you needed six months in order to complete only Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're dealing with Metohija, Professor, what does the word "Metohija" mean, and what is the origin of this word? Where is its root?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: The root goes back to the early middle ages. Metohija comes from the word "Metoh," which means ecclesiastical state, it was a land belonging to a monastery, all of Metohija belonged to the Decani monastery together with a part of Albania and the western part of what is now Montenegro. There are documents and there is a charter from 1330, the document that we translated into English and it is available to the general public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the charter?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: The Decani Charter or the Founding Charter of the Decani Monastery from 1330.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now turn to a different topic. The methodology of a report is how important in your opinion for the conclusion of that report to be drawn?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: The methodology is not important only for the conclusion, it is important for the entire work process, when working on these buildings. Because if the methodology is not correct and if people -- or rather, if methodology is not in compliance with the professional rules, then you will not get a proper result because a proper approach is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you were studying the Herscher and Riedlmayer report, were you able to find what methodology they used and is there any reference to methodology in their report, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Reading the report of Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer, I never came across any methodology that they used and that they referred to. At least I was unable to find any reference to the methodological approach that they used. They never mentioned any methodology applied in their text. If you go out in the field collecting information from non-competent people, basically passers-by, then that is not proper methodology, that is not how the work should be done. There are well-known standards in the protection service. I don't need to remind them. Every profession has it, just like the legal profession, ours does too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, the absence of appropriate methodology ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was: In your opinion does the absence of methodology that should have been defined and adhered to in the report, methodology that is recognised in the profession, can lead to incorrect profession conclusions. So can the absence of this methodology lead to absence of conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, not only are the mistakes possible but they're evident. A lot of time has passed since 1999, it's already 2008, and there have been reports that are contradictory. And nowadays, looking from this distance, we are not able to establish which mosque was destroyed in Pristina. Mr. Riedlmayer and Mr. Herscher name it using one name and other experts use different names. Had they applied the recognised methodology in the professional that mosque could have been identified instantly and now it's been six years and it still hasn't been identified and it's mentioned indeed the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a minute. Have you ever been able to establish whether any mosque in Pristina was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war operations and during the bombing I was in Pristina, and I can tell you that all of us were proud of the fact that not a single cultural and historical monument was damaged. All of us felt proud of it regardless of our ethnic background, because we were happy that there was an area in Kosovo and Metohija that hadn't been damaged. And what we as professionals could observe up until the 12th of June, 1999, in the territory of the Pristina municipality not a single religious building of any provenance was damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are they lying about the damage that they have presented to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't talk about whether they're lying or not. I'm just simply saying that something can be confirmed only on the basis of valid documentation. Where the archives in Pristina was burned, that was on the 13th of June, and that even happened under very suspicious circumstances that I wouldn't like to speculate about. It is almost impossible to accept the explanation provided by the Islamic community, which was absolutely accepted by Mr. Herscher and Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you're talking about when you say that there is disagreement about the identification of the mosque in Pristina that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. You will come across reports stating that it was destroyed and stating that it wasn't destroyed, and that's where the problem lies. When was it destroyed because to claim that it was on the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what you said -- you may be saying that as well, but you did say that there was disagreement about which mosque it was. That's how this started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this is -- there is a causal link. If you start from a wrong premise, then you cannot draw an accurate conclusion. This is why they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. This particular example appears in your report, and you know which building they are talking about. Your evidence suggests there's confusion about the identity of the building in question. Are you saying other experts are talking about some other mosque being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which mosque is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But which mosque are other experts -- tell me which report I can find reference to another mosque in Pristina being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the report of Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer when they say the Vranjevac mosque, and then there is another report where it says it's the mosque called Llap mosque. Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer and the Islamic community all claim that only one mosque was damaged in Pristina, but which one and when; that's the question. It is there that we cannot seem to agree upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which one was it in your -- as a result of your research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the documentation offered to me by both researchers, I'm unable to identify the building. We should start on the basis of documents which would clearly identify the building. None of the authors of reports supported this with any document except that they claim that this was such and such particular building, and that's the wrong methodological approach that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this is something different from the archive, is it, this is a different place that we're talking about from the archive that was burned down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, another place at some 500 metres' distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to indicate for the record that I think the mosque was referred to as being damaged not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness used the word destroyed and that's why I've used the word destroyed, but I note what you say, Mr. Hannis. I, speaking for myself at the moment, Mr. Zecevic, I am not happy about this approach of an expert to giving evidence here dancing around the documents and not actually addressing the real issue, and that is whether mosques were damaged or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me -- let me briefly just respond. You are very well aware of the fact that due to the situation we and our experts or investigators were not able to go on site visit. So therefore, the only way how we could present the expert is to give his evaluation of the report where Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher allegedly went. That was the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I for one do not accept that there is no way of carrying out research in Pristina to establish the damage to mosques. I entirely accept that there may be parts of Kosovo where there are difficulties, but I have freely walked the streets of Pristina myself and therefore I do not accept there's not a methodology available of carrying out research there. I think we are being mocked at the moment, but I'm expressing the view on my behalf only and not on behalf of my colleagues, but I feel I'm being led a merry dance on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Let me also point out that he has a premise and the premise is only confined to documentation, whereas a religious place has a feature, it has a -- all religious places have their features. Now, I mean it could be ascertained from even if it is destroyed or half destroyed from the special features a place has to identify this place as a religious place to any of the groups, and to say that because certain things didn't have the documentation -- I mean, it looks very naive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give my opinion? Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for one second did I challenge that religious buildings were destroyed. I would never make such a mistake. Please trust me. I'm speaking on the basis of professional rules and the confusion that is created if you do not use appropriate methodology and documents, because then we cannot establish the identity of the building and this is where wrong conclusions are drawn. So I'm not denying that these buildings or those buildings were damaged, it would never occur to me to deny that. All I'm saying is that we need to establish specifically what happened, how it happened, under what circumstances, and which particular facility is in question. I don't deny that there was destruction. I'm not going into that because that's not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what's coming over to us at the moment. We are acutely aware of the difficulty of attributing damage to any religious building to any personnel in the case. We know that difficulty, we've mentioned it before, and there is not a great deal of evidence about it. And it's on evidence that's reliable that we will make our decisions. But you -- what we are -- the message we are getting just now is that Riedlmayer and Herscher haven't identified the status of buildings as religious buildings because they haven't got the appropriate documentation, and that's what I'm concerned about that seems to me quite valueless in our work at this stage to be told how difficult our job is - which we know - rather than to be assisted by being told in respect of which particular mosques it might be said that they are not actually religious buildings. This case has long since advanced since Riedlmayer was here and we would hope it had become more focused in that time. Mr. Zecevic, please try to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will endeavour, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in the addendum to your report, annex 11, there is a list of documents -- or rather, a list of all locations that Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer commented upon, that's page 1.223, that's where it starts, 1D743, if we can have it on the screen, please. Could we see e-court page 1.223, 1D743. [In English] Next page, please. This is where it starts. [Interpretation] For illustration purposes we will go over some items. Under 41 of this list, the authors, Riedlmayer and Herscher, use the following name: Tekija Melani Dervis [phoen], the facility under that name, the building known under that name. Can you give us your comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: That building does not exist in documentation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Number 52 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one second. Does it actually exist in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't be able to say whether it exists in fact or not. It is clear that there was major confusion in identifying buildings. There are dozens of such examples throughout the report where one cannot identify the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you don't know the answer to that, is that correct, you don't know if that building exists? Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly don't know because not a single piece of information concerning it was offered to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what evidence is there in this case about that building and how it might have been damaged?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Riedlmayer and Herscher report there is no evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's not in the indictment, so why are we wasting time on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we are trying to illustrate the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but would it not be an idea to illustrate it with one of the mosques about which we have had some evidence and then see the weaknesses there which would really help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, Your Honour, trust me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, but let me inform you what does this mean. Takija is a place which is like a sitting place, it means like a pillow, you know, you sit, squat about; now the name of that person is Melani, and Dervis is a hermit, like you have the Dervis -- so this means a place, this would not be a mosque. This will be a place where this Dervis sat and had his religious things, it may have a room or something else, but Takija Melani Dervis would mean not a mosque but it is a Takija. Thank you. I thought I should inform you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you were going to 52 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm jumping now to a concrete because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and I quite accept I invited you to do that, but 52 is at least an attempt, whatever else you might say, an attempt by the authors to be fair and objective, bearing in mind that the Professor thinks they had an agenda about NATO. But it's certainly not supported by what they say about -- in number 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The point of the matter I would not like to be interpreted as giving evidence instead of the expert here, but according to my knowledge because I was proofing the expert, he has the very same objection as to the previous one. Dzamija Epetimet [phoen] doesn't give a clue and it's not explained so he doesn't -- he doesn't really know about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, that's 51, that's my mistake. I thought it was 52 you were going to. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we prepared some documents anticipating this but we will not be able to use them. Tell me, please, with respect to some of these locations such as the Bajrakli mosque in Pec, did you manage to identify this mosque with an excerpt from the land registry book and other documents? Is there such documentation for the Bajrakli mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and our team used precisely that methodology. Before visiting the building we had all the necessary and valid documentation, including technical documentation, an excerpt from the land registry book, the history, the photograph, and it was not a problem for us to establish the identity of the building and everything connected with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid wasting time that's annex 5 of your report, page 484 in e-court, which refers to the church of St. Nicolas is Djurakovac which also has an excerpt from the land register book and other documents than the church of St. John in Foca --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please, the interpret did not catch the number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you're too quick for the interpreter. Will you go back, please, you will see where the interpretation has stopped. We'll credit you with the time that we've occupied in interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honours. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Let's go back to the church of St. Nicolas in Djurakovac, that's 484 in e-court where there is an excerpt from the land registry book, a description, and a decision; and the same applies to the church of St. John in Velika Hoca from the same document, page 280 in e-court; and also for the monastery of the Vabidenja [phoen] of Our Lady in Dolac, which is on page 494 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. Professor, recently, just a little while ago, you mentioned three mosques, I think, specific mosques, the mosques in Gornje Dobrivo, in Gornje Peduha, Donje Zaberi [phoen], Vlastica, and Celine. As -- well, could you explain to us because of the situation concerning the documents we have been unable to exhibit, we will have to concentrate on the ones my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, has not objected to. So we are now dealing with a mosque in Celine, P2703 [as interpreted], that's a photograph, could we have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number of the exhibit, the interpreter is not absolutely certain she got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P1773, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, on your list of exhibits you wished to add to your 65 ter list, is there any referring to a mosque that has featured in the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Vlastica, Celine, and I'm actually getting to Celine right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Which are these?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mosque in Celine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, which numbers, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- the mosque in Celine is -- are the P77 -- no, those are not -- those are the documents which are -- which are from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I want to know whether on the list you asked us to allow you to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- today, is there any that refers to a mosque that has featured in the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under number 13 of the list, there are three documents, P documents, all P documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, you're -- it's not that, it's your motion I'm talking about, your motion to amend the 65 ter list to include additional exhibits. Do any of these exhibits relate to any mosque that has featured in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honours, just one moment. No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. My conscience remains clear. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, do you see this photograph of a mosque, this is allegedly a mosque that was destroyed in Celine?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court P2445.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the documentation shown to you just a little while ago there was a photograph of a location with a building that had been destroyed, and according to the report by Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer they did not visit the site but they based their report on the photograph. And next to the photograph is this photograph which is said to be a photograph of the mosque before it was destroyed. Professor, based on these two photographs, can you identify this building with the ruin we saw in the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC
utterances.text: Based on these two photographs and the documentation, it's impossible to establish what building this is. I feel very uncomfortable having to say this, I'm uncomfortable because this is a religious building, and I do not want anyone to think for a moment that I have bad intentions or that I want to deny something that actually happened. That is my attitude towards the cultural heritage in general. You saw that we placed the Bajrakli dzamija in the first place on our list, and had this been documented properly for all the buildings this would not have been a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think the two photographs are of the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's impossible to say. I feel very uncomfortable, but the documentation offers by Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer, who did not visit the site at all, and they offered this and the problem is that some of this work was done by amateurs so now there is total confusion in the documentation. You can trust me on this because I spent a lot of time dealing with these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we go back to P1773, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, the bigger picture is P1800, so maybe that should be put together with the P2445. And on the right-hand side if we could have P2445 -- no - in order to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Keep the two photographs. On the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- P1800, please. Okay. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now would you replace that one with P1773, please. No, no, the one on the right with P1773, please. Keep the left as it was. That's not what I want but as long as I get on the left-hand side P1773 that will be satisfactory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Professor Jokic, I'd like to ask you a question. In reaching a finding whether or not it's the same building that was damaged, what characteristics would you look for in the damage in order to be able to reach your finding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on my experience and my insistence on following procedure when identifying buildings, I never did this on my own, I always had a professional photographer accompanying me. A professional photographer knows from what angle he should take a photograph of the building and what markers he should include in the photograph for the building to be identified, and he always takes photographs from several positions. And then there is no doubt because there are markers, so-called markers included, these are nearby buildings, other buildings. And when these photographs are taken from several angles you get all the proper information about the building. Those were the principles and criteria we used for all buildings regardless of their provenance because the profession and the professional approach excludes every other parameter except professional expert parameters. You can find that in our report. All the mosques and Kulas and other buildings that we visited were done according to the methodology as the churches were. And we are always proud to point this out. The European Union recognised the project as valid and gave it an award. Excuse me for saying this but I do have to defend my profession. I am now speaking on behalf of my profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That would be nice. But I would like you to be a little more pointed for me if you could. You look at the picture on the right of a mosque which appears to be intact. What I want to discover from you, when you're looking at the picture on the left what are you looking to see to make you determine whether or not it is one and the same mosque or not as the intact mosque? That is what I really wanted to get from you, what you, the expert and the professional, are looking at the photograph to extract from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speculate but I wouldn't like to do that because if everything had been done properly there would have been no doubt. Had the picture been taken professionally even a lay person would have been able to establish what this was, but I would like to refrain from answering this because it would be against my conscience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Professor, I have a question for you. Do you know the difference between a mosque and a "dzamija"? You mentioned about the "dzamija" in the past, you mentioned it again. Your learned counsel also mentioned it at page 82, line 16. What is the difference between "dzamija" and mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there is a difference in architecture and in the purpose for which the building is used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What is the purpose of a "dzamija"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, both are religious buildings, both a mosque and a "dzamija" are religious buildings, but a "dzamija" is a building where religious ceremonies are carried out more extensively and in larger number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to tell you that this is not correct. "Dzamija" is the seminary. It's a place where students get education, and side by side they're also praying there. So that's the "dzamija." Dzamija Islamija, this famous one in Cairo, Al-Azhar and various places. So "dzamija" is not what you are thinking. So this is the problem because had you studied this and then went on discovering whether there is a building which doesn't have the feature of a mosque but is a religious place or where religion is taught, I think things must have been much simpler. Now, "dzamija" is a seminary and a "dzamija" Azhar the famous place in Cairo. So "dzamija" is that, again in this picture on the left it could have been very -- it could have been easily discovered whether this is the demolished mosque or not because there would be the residual parts of the minaret somewhere lying here, those could have been seen and discovered, there would have been the signs of the mijrab and so on and so forth. As an expert you should have seen that. I'm very sorry to have treaded on that line, but I thought I should at least inquire from you your expertise on the subject. I apologise if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think perhaps I've understood things rather differently from my colleague. I thought the very point you were making was that no one had actually gone to look at the site to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not your point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my point, nobody went on site to check, but I wish to thank His Honour for his explanation, which I fully accept. But in the case of Kosovo and Metohija even a practicing religious ethnic Albanian will not be able to explain this to you and would not know this. Of course I fully appreciate your knowledge of this issue, but unfortunately in Kosovo that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have to end our proceedings for today at this stage, Professor, and resume them tomorrow. That will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom. I'm sorry about that, but you will require to return then to complete your evidence. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt the examination by Mr. Zecevic, but I wanted to give a comment for the record. We were prevented from doing our work in Pristina. We were unable to move throughout the town, unable to move throughout Kosovo. As soon as we were identified as to who we are, we became unsafe -- it became unsafe for us to work there and this was confirmed to us by representatives of authorities, including representatives of UNMIK. That's what I wanted to say and I wanted to make sure that that's recorded in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I also want to make it clear to you, Mr. Visnjic, that we have not had it brought to our attention that you had difficulties in Pristina, and also to make it clear to you that there is more than one way to skin a cat and that there are other ways of carrying out investigations in Pristina that are not provocative or cannot even be considered to begin to begin to be provocative as long as you engage the right people to carry out your inquiries in the right way then you will achieve your objective. No inquiry was made of us for assistance to enable you to carry out inquiries there. We would take a very firm stance on any impediment to inquiries. You know also the efforts we made before when you ran into personal difficulties which ought never to have beset you, but our efforts in that regard were not exhausted and I -- we don't accept that we have not done what we can and would have done more to ensure that your inquiries were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm grateful to the Trial Chamber, and I didn't address the Chamber. I just wanted the fact to be recorded. As soon as one of us is identified as the person doing its work there, then we could encounter certain problems, safety-related, and I wanted that to be recorded. Now, whether this was something to be -- this was something that should have been done by an expert or an investigator engaged by us, we can make our own conclusions regarding that. But I wanted to make sure that this is officially on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's on the record with clear reservations about the extent to which you exhausted the possibilities open to you. We'll adjourn now and we'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
